content: The question of whether supplemental oxygen should be discontinued abruptly or gradually in preterm or low birth weight infants remains a topic of debate. Studies conducted on both human and animal models have yielded inconsistent findings regarding the impact of these two methods on critical infant outcomes. The primary objective of this investigation was to evaluate the effects of gradual versus abrupt discontinuation of supplemental oxygen on several key outcomes, including mortality, the development of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), lung function, growth, and overall development in preterm or low birth weight infants. To address this, the researchers employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. This involved a comprehensive review of multiple sources, including the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, MEDLINE, prior reviews with cross-references, conference abstracts, symposia proceedings, and expert consultations. Additional searches were conducted in the MEDLINE and CINAHL databases to identify any relevant trials not already included in the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (CENTRAL/CCTR). The inclusion criteria for this review required that all studies utilize random or quasi-random allocation of patients and directly compare gradual weaning with abrupt discontinuation of supplemental oxygen in preterm or low birth weight infants. The methodological quality of the eligible studies was independently assessed by each author, focusing on potential biases related to selection, performance, attrition, and detection. Data extraction and review were also conducted independently by the authors, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion. Data analysis adhered to the rigorous standards established by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. The systematic review included one small trial involving 51 infants. The findings from this trial demonstrated a significant reduction in the incidence of severe retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), specifically vascular retrolental fibroplasia, in infants who were gradually weaned from high oxygen concentrations compared to those who experienced abrupt discontinuation. The relative risk (RR) was calculated at 0.22, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.07 to 0.68. Importantly, this reduction in severe ROP was observed regardless of the duration of oxygen therapy. The authors concluded that the results of this systematic review provide further evidence supporting the association between routine exposure to high ambient oxygen levels in the early neonatal period and the development of ROP in preterm or low birth weight infants. However, due to the small sample size of the included trial and the historical nature of oxygen monitoring techniques used, the findings offer limited guidance for clinicians in determining the optimal method—gradual or abrupt—for weaning oxygen in contemporary neonatal care settings.
